title: The Cruelty and Futility of Criminalizing the Homeless
author: Farrah Hassen
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/IMG_1282-680x510.jpeg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/06/26/the-
cruelty-and-futility-of-criminalizing-the-homeless/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/06/IMG_1282-680x510.jpeg)

Sign at homeless camp, Grants Pass, Oregon. Photo: Jeffrey St. Clair.

Two years ago this summer, the Supreme Court paved the way for more states and
cities to fine or jail people for the “crime” of not having a roof over their
head.

In their June 28, 2024 _Grants Pass_ _v. Johnson_
[decision](https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/23pdf/23-175_19m2.pdf), the
court ruled that an Oregon city’s ordinance barring people from sleeping in
public, even when shelter is unavailable, was not “cruel and unusual
punishment.”

Since then, [more than 300
cities](https://housingnothandcuffs.org/2026/04/22/statement04222026/) have
passed bills criminalizing unhoused people. Statehouses have also followed
suit. In April, Indiana’s governor
[signed](https://www.wlky.com/article/indiana-ban-public-camping-
statewide/71088352) a statewide prohibition on sleeping in public spaces
punishable by up to $500 in fines and 60 days in jail.

Louisiana, which has the nation’s highest rates of both
[incarceration](https://www.prisonpolicy.org/profiles/LA.html) and
[poverty](https://www.americashealthrankings.org/explore/measures/household_poverty/LA),
is the latest to embrace this cruel and counterproductive approach. The
state’s [recent](https://www.kadn.com/news/local/gov-landry-signs-
controversial-law-criminalizing-sleeping-on-
streets/article_2cd586ee-c75c-4643-b17f-771a3c8a0ea9.html) “[Streets to
Success Act](https://legis.la.gov/Legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1481225)”
criminalizes sleeping in public spaces with fines up to $500 and six months of
imprisonment.

The legislation also creates a “Homelessness Court” which will divert some
people to a year-long [mandatory treatment
program](https://legis.la.gov/Legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1481225)to avoid jail
time — but they would still be required to [plead
guilty](https://legis.la.gov/Legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1481225) and pay for
treatment. The court can mandate unpaid labor for those unable to pay, and
failure to complete the program could still result in a jail sentence.

Far from reducing homelessness, a criminal record makes it _more_ difficult
for people to find employment, remain financially secure, and get into stable
housing.

The _Grants Pass_ decision has normalized the dehumanization of people living
unhoused. Over the past two years, localities have [ramped
up](https://www.themarshallproject.org/2025/11/20/california-police-homeless-
los-angeles) the forced clearing of encampments, where many people live when
they have no other choice. Alongside other
[harms](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2803839?guestAccessKey=f321ceca-78d6-4d55-bcc5-e7a775ce1152),
these “sweeps” have resulted in authorities [unlawfully seizing and
destroying](https://www.kqed.org/news/12049434/sf-agrees-to-2-8-million-
settlement-plans-reform-of-homeless-encampment-sweeps) unhoused people’s
survival gear and personal items.

Last July, President Trump issued an [executive
order](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/07/ending-crime-
and-disorder-on-americas-streets/) urging cities and states to forcibly
institutionalize unhoused people to “restore public order.” The administration
is [shifting](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/06/02/us/politics/housing-first-
homeless-hud.html?unlocked_article_code=1.sVA.dGSJ.7G2ckD-knh3F&smid=nytcore-
android-share) significant funds away from long-term housing to short-term
transitional housing with treatment mandates.

Forced treatment is constitutionally questionable to say the least. Short-term
aid centered on treatment is also less
[effective](https://nlihc.org/sites/default/files/Housing-First-Evidence.pdf)
at reducing homelessness than the bipartisan [Housing
First](https://endhomelessness.org/resources/toolkits-and-training-
materials/housing-first/) approach, which provides permanent housing _without_
preconditions, along with voluntary supportive services to help people improve
their well-being.

Penalizing people fails to address the root of homelessness: the lack of
affordable, permanent, and adequate housing. “I’m working, but I can’t afford
to stay in the house,” Christopher Brumfield
[told](https://capitalbnews.org/louisiana-homelessness-bill-jail-hard-labor/)
_Capital B_ in New Orleans. He’s been living unhoused “on and off” since 2020.

Since _Grants Pass_ , the cost of living has only [gone
up.](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/cost-of-living-income-quality-of-life/) Half
of all renters [pay
more](https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/sites/default/files/reports/files/Harvard_JCHS_Americas_Rental_Housing_2026.pdf)
than what they can afford. Rising health care and housing costs leave more
people one emergency away from falling into homelessness.

Meanwhile, Trump’s “Big Beautiful Bill” has slashed funding for social safety
net programs like SNAP and Medicaid in favor of tax breaks for billionaires.
His [proposed cuts to affordable housing and homelessness
programs](https://nlihc.org/resource/president-trump-releases-fy27-budget-
request-proposing-significant-cuts-hud-programs-and) threaten housing support
for families, veterans, people with disabilities, and seniors. Even the
[modest progress](https://endhomelessness.org/media/news-releases/long-
awaited-federal-data-shows-the-first-overall-reduction-in-homelessness-
since-2016/) made during the Biden administration to reduce homelessness is at
risk.

Homelessness is a policy choice, not a personal failing. We can overcome it if
our government finally treats housing as a[fundamental human
right](https://www.ohchr.org/en/special-procedures/sr-housing/human-right-
adequate-housing) for all people, instead of a commodity controlled by
billionaire investors and corporate landlords.

Permanently affordable housing under public control, known as social housing,
has achieved[ positive
results](https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2024/jan/10/the-social-
housing-secret-how-vienna-became-the-worlds-most-livable-city) in Vienna,
Austria. U.S. cities would stand to benefit from this human rights-centered
housing solution combined with stronger tenant protections and community-based
health services.

Housing for all requires sustained investment, but it’s the foundation for
creating safe and healthy communities. Plus, it [costs
less](https://www.urban.org/features/housing-first-breaks-homelessness-jail-
cycle) to house people and fund the services they need than to jail them. As
Shana, a dental hygienist from Louisiana who once lived unhoused, [put
it](https://www.facebook.com/reel/2596676374061436), “The solution isn’t a
cell. It’s a front door.”

Homeless](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/06/26/the-cruelty-and-futility-of-
